findings.description: USERNAME_SAFE, PASSWORD_SAFE, and USERINFO_SAFE (and also FRAG_SAFE/QUERY_SAFE/PATH_SAFE) never exclude the '%' character (0x25) from the 'safe' set passed to quote(). As a result, a literal '%' in a username/password is no longer percent-encoded, whereas previously `quote(userinfo, safe=SUB_DELIMS + ':')` did escape it. This is demonstrated by the modified test `test_url_copywith_userinfo_subcomponents`, where the expected output changed from '...%20%25@...' to '...%20%@...' (trailing %25 became a bare %). Leaving '%' unescaped breaks round-trip safety: e.g. a password like 'abc%20to' would now be left as-is by quote(), and later when the stored userinfo is unquoted (e.g. via the `.password` property, or by any downstream consumer that re-parses the URL), '%20' would be decoded as a space, silently corrupting the original credential value.
findings.suggestion: Explicitly exclude 0x25 ('%') from USERNAME_SAFE, PASSWORD_SAFE, and USERINFO_SAFE (and consider doing the same for PATH_SAFE/QUERY_SAFE/FRAG_SAFE) so that raw '%' characters supplied by the caller are always percent-encoded to '%25', guaranteeing that encode/decode round-trips correctly for arbitrary input. Update the test to assert the correct, escaped output rather than the regressed one.

findings.description: Because '%' is treated as a 'safe' character when encoding username/password/userinfo, a value containing a sequence that looks like a percent-escape (e.g. '%2F', '%0d%0a') will not be re-encoded and can be mis-interpreted as an actual percent-escape by this or any downstream URL parser/proxy that decodes it. This class of inconsistency between how different components/parsers interpret ambiguous percent sequences is a known source of URL-parsing confusion/request-smuggling/auth-bypass style bugs, so silently allowing unescaped '%' in credential components is risky.
findings.suggestion: Always percent-encode literal '%' characters in username/password/userinfo input (i.e., never include 0x25 in the safe set for these components) to eliminate the ambiguity, matching the previous, safer behavior.

findings.description: USERNAME_SAFE and PASSWORD_SAFE are built with identical, fully duplicated list comprehensions (same excluded tuple). This duplication makes it easy for the two definitions to silently drift apart in future edits.
findings.suggestion: Define the excluded-codepoint tuple once and derive both constants from it, e.g. `PASSWORD_SAFE = USERNAME_SAFE`, or share a single `_USERINFO_EXCLUDED` tuple used to build both.

findings.description: The local variables `fragment`/`parsed_fragment` were renamed to `frag`/`parsed_frag` with no apparent functional reason, adding unrelated diff noise and reducing readability/consistency with the rest of the codebase (which otherwise spells out `fragment`).
findings.suggestion: Keep the original `fragment`/`parsed_fragment` naming to minimize unrelated changes and preserve readability.

findings.description: The five safe-character sets are each built by repeating a growing, hand-copied tuple of excluded code points, which is error-prone (e.g. it's easy to miscopy one of the many hex literals) and obscures the layered relationship described in the WHATWG spec (fragment ⊂ query ⊂ path ⊂ userinfo).
findings.suggestion: Build these sets incrementally using set union of previously-defined exclusion sets (e.g. `PATH_EXCLUDE = QUERY_EXCLUDE | {0x3F, 0x60, 0x7B, 0x7D}`), which better documents the hierarchy and reduces the chance of transcription errors.

findings.description: No new tests were added to validate the newly introduced WHATWG-based encode sets. The only related test that changed (`test_url_copywith_userinfo_subcomponents`) was updated to assert the new, under-escaped output ('%' instead of '%25') rather than flagging it as unexpected, so the regression around unescaped '%' slips through untested.
findings.suggestion: Add explicit tests that: (1) confirm '%' in username/password/path/query/fragment input is always percent-encoded to '%25', and (2) perform round-trip checks (e.g. `httpx.URL(str(url)).password == original_password`) for values containing characters like '%', '#', '?', '`', '{', '}', etc., to catch regressions in the escaping rules going forward.

summary: This PR refactors httpx's percent-encoding rules to align with the WHATWG URL spec's percent-encode sets for fragment/query/path/userinfo, replacing the old ad-hoc GEN_DELIMS/WHATWG_SAFE logic. The new sets are correctly derived from the spec for the delimiter characters, but all of the new 'safe' character sets omit '%' (0x25) from the excluded code points. For path/query/fragment this preserves prior behavior (the old WHATWG_SAFE string already included '%'), but for username/password/userinfo this is a behavioral regression versus the previous `SUB_DELIMS + ':'` safe set, which *did* escape '%'. The accompanying test change in test_url.py confirms this: the expected output changed from a properly escaped trailing '%25' to a raw, unescaped trailing '%', i.e. the test was updated to codify the regression rather than catch it. Leaving '%' unescaped breaks round-trip safety for arbitrary user-supplied credentials/components (e.g. a password literally containing '%2F' would silently become '/' when later unquoted), which is both a correctness and a security concern for credential handling.

findings.description: The new comment mentions that `verify` can be a string path to a CA bundle file, but doesn't mention that it can also be a path to a directory of CA certificates (as supported by underlying urllib3/OpenSSL), which is also a valid documented usage pattern in requests.
findings.suggestion: Consider expanding the doc comment to mention that verify can be a path to either a CA bundle file or a directory containing CA certificates, matching the broader documentation elsewhere (e.g., in requests' top-level docs) for consistency.

findings.description: No test coverage is needed or added since this is a documentation-only change, but there is no verification that this new docstring text matches the actual public API documentation (e.g., docs/user/advanced.rst) which may already describe this behavior elsewhere, risking duplication or inconsistency.
findings.suggestion: Cross-check with existing documentation (README, docs/) to ensure consistency and avoid duplicate/conflicting descriptions of the verify parameter.

summary: This PR adds a documentation comment clarifying that the `verify` attribute of `Session` can also accept a string path to a CA bundle file, in addition to the boolean True/False values already documented. The change is purely a docstring/comment addition with no functional code changes, so overall risk is minimal.

findings.description: The previous implementation suppressed the 'Trying to detect' UserWarning emitted by charset_normalizer via `warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", "Trying to detect", module="charset_normalizer")` when chardet was unavailable and charset_normalizer was used as a fallback. This filter has been dropped in the refactor, so users who only have charset_normalizer installed (no chardet) may now see this warning resurface whenever encoding is auto-detected, which is a behavioral regression from the prior release.
findings.suggestion: Re-add the warning suppression for charset_normalizer's 'Trying to detect' message (e.g. in compat.py's _resolve_char_detection, or wherever charset_normalizer is selected as the fallback), so behavior matches the previous release.

findings.description: apparent_encoding now silently falls back to 'utf-8' when no detection library is present, rather than failing loudly. While this is the intended behavior of the PR, decoding content as UTF-8 for arbitrary/unknown encodings can silently produce corrupted/mojibake text for non-UTF-8 responses, and the docstring for apparent_encoding was not updated to mention this fallback behavior, which could confuse users.
findings.suggestion: Update the apparent_encoding docstring to document the utf-8 fallback behavior when no detection library is installed, and consider whether this silent fallback could mask real encoding bugs for users who forgot to install a detection library.

findings.description: _resolve_char_detection() keeps iterating over the remaining library names even after chardet has been successfully resolved; the `if chardet is None` guard only prevents re-importing but still executes the loop body/condition check needlessly, and depends on iteration order with a somewhat indirect early-exit pattern.

No unit tests are included in the diff that explicitly exercise the new code paths: apparent_encoding falling back to 'utf-8' when chardet is None, the RequestsDependencyWarning being raised instead of an exception in check_compatibility, and packages.py behaving correctly when chardet is None. The new CI job (no_chardet) exercises the full test suite without these libraries installed, but it's not clear existing tests actually assert on the new fallback/warning behavior specifically.
findings.suggestion: Add explicit unit tests that mock/patch requests.compat.chardet to None and assert: (1) Response.apparent_encoding returns 'utf-8', (2) check_compatibility emits RequestsDependencyWarning rather than raising, and (3) requests.packages still imports successfully without chardet/charset_normalizer.

summary: This PR makes chardet/charset_normalizer optional dependencies: instead of raising an exception when neither library is available, requests now emits a RequestsDependencyWarning and falls back to "utf-8" for apparent_encoding. The compat.py module was refactored to dynamically resolve whichever detection library is installed, and packages.py/models.py were updated to tolerate chardet being None. A new CI job verifies the library still works with neither dependency installed. Overall the change is reasonable and well-contained, but there are a few regressions and gaps worth addressing.
